deed: Paul Berg won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his groundbreaking research on nucleic acids
title: Paul Berg joined DNA from two organisms, led the Asilomar Conference and won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry

trailer.text: Paul Berg, a biochemist at Stanford University who was born in Brooklyn to Jewish immigrant parents from Russia, won the 1980 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
According to the Nobel Foundation, he created the first DNA molecule made of parts from different organisms.
Soon afterwards he faced public fears of the creation of new plagues, and led a call for a voluntary moratorium on the research.

In February 1975 he organized the Asilomar Conference with David Baltimore, Sydney Brenner, Richard Roblin and Maxine Singer, and there it was decided that the research would continue under stringent restrictions.
According to the Nobel Foundation, his method opened the way to bacteria that produce substances for medicines.

paragraphs.text: Paul Berg was born on June 30, 1926, in Brooklyn, New York, the son of Jewish immigrant parents from Russia.
He told JTA that he grew up in the Sea Gate section of Brooklyn, where he had his bar mitzvah.

According to him, the ambition to become a scientist took shape already in junior high school, partly through reading, and in high school it was nurtured by Sophie Wolfe, who was in charge of the stockroom for the chemistry, physics and biology classes and started after-school science clubs.
Berg said that he felt a need to contribute to the war effort, and therefore enlisted in the Navy to become a pilot.
He completed an undergraduate degree in biochemistry at Penn State in 1948, and received a PhD in biochemistry from Western Reserve University (now Case Western Reserve) in 1952.
According to him, he was among the first to show in vitro that folic acid and vitamin B12 cofactors participate in one-carbon metabolic processes.
In Copenhagen he and Wolfgang Joklik discovered a new enzyme that created nucleoside triphosphates for the assembly of nucleic acids.
Berg moved to Stanford to help Arthur Kornberg, who also won a Nobel Prize, set up the new department of biochemistry.
From 1969 to 1974 he headed the department.
Berg said that he conceived the idea of using the SV40 virus to introduce new genes into mammalian cells.
According to the Nobel Foundation, he succeeded in inserting DNA from a bacterium into the DNA of the virus.

According to the Science History Institute, in Berg's 1971 experiment the closed loops of the DNA of the bacterial virus lambda and of the virus SV40 were cut, each loop in one place, using the enzyme EcoRI.
Berg wrote that his team inserted into the genome of SV40 a DNA segment containing three genes of the bacterium E. coli responsible for the metabolism of the sugar galactose.
According to the Nobel Foundation, this created the first DNA molecule made of parts from different organisms.
According to the original 1972 PNAS paper by Berg and colleagues, the DNA segment inserted into the SV40 virus contained genes of the lambda phage and the galactose operon of the bacterium E. coli.
Soon after he joined DNA from two organisms, Berg faced public fears of the creation of new plagues.
According to the US National Library of Medicine, science fiction scenarios fed these fears.
Berg wrote that there were speculations that normally harmless bacteria would be changed and cause disease in humans.
Even before Berg's 1972 paper was published, his colleague Robert Pollack worried that lab workers would be at risk if recombinants with tumor genes reached cultures.

Berg wrote that several scientists feared that bacteria carrying SV40 DNA would escape and cause cancer in people infected with them, and so he and his team chose to postpone their experiments until it was clear that there was no risk.
According to him, those who sounded the alarm were not politicians or journalists but scientists.
Berg wrote that in mid-1974 he led a committee that conveyed the concerns to the president of the US National Academy of Sciences.
On July 26, 1974, the letter known as the "Berg letter" appeared in the journal Science.
According to Stanford, Berg led a call for a voluntary moratorium, that is, a self-imposed halt, on genetic engineering research.
According to the National Library of Medicine, it was the first voluntary moratorium in the history of science, and everyone observed it.
In February 1975 the Asilomar Conference on recombinant DNA was held, organized by Berg, David Baltimore, Sydney Brenner, Richard Roblin and Maxine Singer.
The conference was held at the Asilomar Conference Center in Pacific Grove, California.
It was attended by scientists from several countries, as well as lawyers, journalists and government officials.
Berg wrote that the agenda had to focus on an assessment of the risks.
According to him, the debate turned around when it was suggested to estimate the risk of each type of experiment, and to set safety guidelines according to the level of risk.
On the final day of the conference the participants agreed that the research would continue, but under stringent restrictions.
The conference's recommendations formed the basis of the official US guidelines, issued in July 1976.
According to the Nobel Foundation, Berg's method opened the way to bacteria that produce substances for medicines.
According to Britannica, one of the first practical results was a strain of bacteria carrying the gene for the hormone insulin.
According to Professor P. J. Utz, insulin for diabetic patients comes from a recombinant source, and this was made possible by Berg's work.
According to Stanford Magazine, Berg's discoveries helped launch the biotech industry, and led to hepatitis vaccines and synthetic insulin.
Berg wrote that hormones, vaccines, drugs and diagnostic tools are improving medicine.
He also wrote that without the tools of recombinant DNA, the genome of humans or of any other organism would not have been sequenced.
Professor Paul Babitzke of Penn State said that cutting DNA with restriction enzymes and joining it with ligase revolutionized experiments in molecular biology.
Nobel laureate Brian Kobilka said that he benefited from the ability to manipulate DNA for practical purposes.
Berg wrote that over the 33 years since Asilomar, many experiments with recombinant DNA had been carried out without reported incidents.
According to him, no hazard to public health from the applications of the technology has been documented.
The 1980 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Berg for his fundamental studies of the biochemistry of nucleic acids, with particular regard to recombinant DNA.
The other half of the prize was awarded jointly to Walter Gilbert and Frederick Sanger.
According to JTA, Berg, then 54, of Stanford University, received half of the prize, which amounted to 215 thousand dollars.
JTA described Berg and Gilbert as two Jewish American scientists.
In the same year, 1980, Berg also won the Lasker Award in Basic Science for cloning genes.
In 1983 President Ronald Reagan presented him with the National Medal of Science.
In 2005 he received the Biotechnology Heritage Award from the Chemical Heritage Foundation.
He was a member of the National Academy of Sciences, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the Royal Society of London.
He twice won the Henry Kaiser Award for Excellence in Teaching at the Stanford School of Medicine.
In 1971 Berg lectured for ten days at the Weizmann Institute in Rehovot.
He told JTA that Israel is a miracle, and an astonishing country because of what it has been able to achieve.
According to his colleagues, Berg always declined to patent his findings, and shared information even before publication.
According to Chemistry World, Berg estimated that Stanford earned more than one hundred million dollars over 17 years from the patents on recombinant DNA.
He disputed the title father of genetic engineering, and said that they had made only the first step.
Berg raised more than $50 million for the Beckman Center building, which opened in 1989, and directed the center until 2000.
He raised another $4 million for the Li Ka Shing Center for Learning and Knowledge.
According to Chemistry World, he published more than 200 scientific articles and retired from research in 2000.
In 2004 Berg promoted California Proposition 71, which created the California Institute of Regenerative Medicine.
That same year he was one of 20 Nobel laureates who signed an open letter accusing the Bush administration of relying on bad science.
His wife, Mildred, died before him.
Berg died on February 15, 2023, at his home on the Stanford University campus, at the age of 96.
Berg wrote that the Asilomar conference reached its conclusion not without outspoken opposition from some of its prominent participants.
According to him, there was criticism that the conference did not discuss the ethical and legal implications of genetic engineering of plants, animals and humans.
He also wrote that in the 1970s there was criticism of scientists who took it upon themselves to lead in formulating policies on matters of public concern.

disagreements.question: In what year was the DNA-joining experiment carried out?

versions.says: Nobel Foundation: in 1972 Berg succeeded in inserting DNA from a bacterium into the DNA of the virus
Science History Institute: the experiment was carried out in 1971

disagreements.question: How many days did the Asilomar Conference last?

versions.says: National Library of Medicine: four days
Berg, on the Nobel website: three days

disagreements.question: How many participants were at the conference?

versions.says: National Library of Medicine: 150 scientists from several countries, as well as lawyers
Berg wrote that about 140 people took part in the conference, among them scientists, lawyers, journalists and government officials.

disagreements.question: What share of the participants were from the media?

versions.says: National Library of Medicine: 16 journalists covered the conference
Berg, on the Nobel website: more than 10% of the participants
Berg, in Nature: about 15% of the participants

disagreements.question: How many years did Berg's marriage last?

versions.says: The Scientist: nearly 75 years of marriage, until her death in 2021

disagreements.question: Where did Berg's family come from?

versions.says: Stanford and Chemistry World: his parents were Jews who immigrated from Russia
JTA: his forebears came to the US from Ukraine

unknowns.text: We do not know exactly what Berg taught during the ten days at the Weizmann Institute

claims.text: לפי עמיתיו, ברג סירב תמיד לרשום פטנט על ממצאיו ושיתף מידע לפני פרסום.
claims.quote: He always declined to patent his findings and shared information in advance of publication, a rarity in an often-secretive field.

claims.text: לפי Chemistry World, ברג העריך שסטנפורד הרוויחה יותר ממאה מיליון דולר במשך 17 שנה מהפטנטים על DNA רקומביננטי.
claims.quote: Berg estimated that Stanford probably earned more than $100 million over the course of 17 years from these patents.

claims.text: ברג חלק על התיאור שלו כ"אבי ההנדסה הגנטית" ואמר שהם עשו רק את הצעד הראשון.
claims.quote: we made only the first step and everybody else seized immediately on this new technology

claims.text: ברג גייס יותר מ-50 מיליון דולר לבניין מרכז בקמן, שנפתח ב-1989, וניהל את המרכז עד 2000.
claims.quote: He raised more than $50 million for the building, which opened in 1989, and he served as director of the center until 2000

claims.text: ברג גייס 4 מיליון דולר למרכז לי קא שינג ללמידה וידע.
claims.quote: Berg raised $4 million for the Li Ka Shing Center for Learning and Knowledge

claims.text: לפי Chemistry World, ברג פרסם מעל 200 מאמרים מדעיים ופרש מהמחקר ב-2000.
claims.quote: He published over 200 scientific articles throughout his career, retiring from research in 2000.

claims.text: ב-2004 ברג קידם את הצעה 71 בקליפורניה, שהקימה את המכון לרפואה רגנרטיבית של קליפורניה.
claims.quote: in 2004 he promoted California Proposition 71, which created the California Institute of Regenerative Medicine

claims.text: ברג היה אחד מ-20 חתני נובל שחתמו ב-2004 על מכתב פתוח שהאשים את ממשל בוש בהסתמכות על מדע גרוע.
claims.quote: Berg was one of 20 Nobel laureates who signed a 2004 open letter accusing the Bush administration of citing bad science to support policy decisions.

claims.text: לפי מגזין סטנפורד, אשתו של ברג, מילדרד, הלכה לעולמה לאחר 74 שנות נישואים.
claims.quote: Berg was predeceased by his wife of 74 years, Mildred.

claims.text: ברג מת ב-15 בפברואר בביתו בקמפוס סטנפורד, בגיל 96.
claims.quote: died Feb. 15 at his home on the Stanford University campus, surrounded by loved ones. He was 96.

claims.text: ברג כתב שהכנס הגיע למסקנתו לא בלי התנגדות חריפה של חלק ממשתתפיו הבולטים.
claims.quote: not without outspoken opposition from some of its more notable participants

claims.text: ברג כתב שנשמעה ביקורת על כך שכנס אסילומר לא דן בהשלכות האתיות והמשפטיות של הנדסה גנטית בצמחים, בבעלי חיים ובבני אדם.
claims.quote: An often-voiced criticism of the Asilomar Conference discussions was the failure to consider the ethical and legal implications of genetic engineering of plants, animals and humans.

claims.text: ברג כתב שבשנות ה-70 נשמעה ביקורת על מדענים שנטלו הנהגה בעיצוב מדיניות בענייני ציבור.
claims.quote: Frequently heard in the 1970s were criticisms of scientists for assuming leadership in formulating policies that were matters of public concern.

claims.text: לפי ספריית הרפואה הלאומית, 16 עיתונאים סיקרו את הכנס בן ארבעת הימים.
claims.quote: to help consider legal and ethical issues, and 16 journalists to cover the four-day event

claims.text: ברג כתב שיותר מ-10% מהמשתתפים היו מהתקשורת.
claims.quote: more than 10% of the participants were from the news media

claims.text: במאמר אחר כתב ברג שכ-15% מהמשתתפים באסילומר היו מהתקשורת.
claims.quote: Because some 15% of the participants at Asilomar were from the media

claims.text: לפי The Scientist, אשתו של ברג מתה ב-2021 לאחר כמעט 75 שנות נישואים.
claims.quote: His wife of nearly 75 years preceded him in death in 2021.

claims.text: לפי המאמר המקורי של ברג ועמיתיו ב-PNAS משנת 1972, קטע ה-DNA שהוחדר לנגיף SV40 הכיל גנים של הנגיף למבדה ואת אופרון הגלקטוז של החיידק E. coli.
claims.quote: DNA segment containing lambda phage genes and the galactose operon

claims.text: בפברואר 1975 נערך כנס אסילומר בנושא DNA רקומביננטי, שאורגן על ידי ברג, דייוויד בולטימור, סידני ברנר, ריצ'רד רובלין ומקסין סינגר.
claims.quote: David Baltimore, Sydney Brenner, Richard Roblin and Maxine Singer
claims.checker_note: audit: quote found on the fetched page

claims.text: בפברואר 1975 ארגן עם דייוויד בולטימור, סידני ברנר, ריצ'רד רובלין ומקסין סינגר את כנס אסילומר, ושם הוחלט שהמחקר יימשך תחת הגבלות מחמירות.
claims.quote: David Baltimore, Sydney Brenner, Richard Roblin and Maxine Singer
claims.checker_note: audit: quote found on the fetched page

claims.text: ברג כתב שהצוות שלו החדיר לגנום של SV40 קטע DNA שהכיל שלושה גנים של החיידק E. coli האחראים לחילוף החומרים של הסוכר גלקטוז.
claims.quote: we inserted a segment of DNA containing three Escherichia coli genes responsible for the metabolism of the sugar galactose into the genome of the Simian Virus
claims.checker_note: audit: quote found on the fetched page

claims.text: הוא סיים תואר ראשון בביוכימיה בפנסילבניה סטייט ב-1948, וקיבל דוקטורט בביוכימיה מאוניברסיטת ווסטרן ריזרב (כיום קייס ווסטרן ריזרב) ב-1952.
claims.quote: his doctorate from Western Reserve University in 1952
